lessons.title: Module 10 Lesson 1: Setting Up a Profitable Plumbing Business in Africa
lessons.body: Starting a plumbing business in Africa is not just about fixing pipes. It is about solving urgent water and sanitation problems for households, businesses, and institutions that often have no reliable alternative. The demand is constant. In many cities and towns, municipal water supply is intermittent, pipe networks are aging, and new construction is booming. That combination creates steady work for plumbers who can show up on time, diagnose accurately, and charge fairly. This lesson focuses on the business side: how to structure your plumbing enterprise so it generates profit from day one. First, understand your market. In most African cities, you will find three main customer groups: residential clients, commercial clients such as hotels, schools, and restaurants, and institutional clients like NGOs, churches, and government agencies. Residential work is easier to win but often lower value. Commercial and institutional work pays better but requires documentation, insurance, and sometimes bidding. Start with residential and small commercial jobs to build cash flow, then use that experience to pursue larger contracts. Your legal setup matters. Register your business with the relevant authority in your country. In Kenya, that means the eCitizen portal and a business name or limited company registration. In Nigeria, the Corporate Affairs Commission. In Ghana, the Registrar General. In South Africa, the CIPC. Registration allows you to open a business bank account, issue proper invoices, and qualify for contracts. It also protects your personal assets if you form a limited company. Do not skip this step because a customer asks for a receipt and you cannot provide one. Next, decide on your service model. You can operate as a solo plumber, a small team with one or two apprentices, or a full-service company with multiple vans and a dispatcher. Most successful African plumbing businesses start small and grow through referrals. Your reputation is your marketing budget. Every job you complete well is a future job through word of mouth. Create a simple pricing structure. Charge a call-out fee that covers your transport and initial inspection. Then quote labor and materials separately. Many plumbers lose money because they bundle everything into one price and underestimate material costs. Keep a price list for common jobs: replacing a tap washer, unblocking a drain, installing a geyser, fixing a toilet cistern, and repairing a burst pipe. Update this list every three months because material prices in Africa can change quickly due to exchange rates and fuel costs. Cash flow is the lifeblood of a plumbing business. You need money to buy materials before the customer pays you. Start with a small float and build relationships with local hardware suppliers. Ask for trade discounts and credit terms of seven to fourteen days. If you can buy materials on credit and get paid by the customer within three days, you can grow without borrowing. Keep records of every job: date, customer name, address, description of work, materials used, labor charge, and payment status. A simple notebook works at the start, but move to a spreadsheet or phone app as soon as possible. Marketing on a budget is possible. Create a WhatsApp Business profile with your services, location, and photos of completed work. Ask satisfied customers for a Google review or a testimonial you can share. Print simple business cards and leave them with hardware stores, real estate agents, and property managers. In many African communities, the local church, mosque, or community group is a powerful referral network. Attend meetings, be visible, and offer to help with small repairs at community buildings. That goodwill translates into paid work. Finally, protect yourself. Get public liability insurance if you can afford it. It covers damage to a customer property, such as flooding a room while fixing a pipe. Also insure your tools and vehicle. In countries where the informal sector is large, insurance may seem expensive, but one accident can wipe out your savings. Set aside a small percentage of every payment for an emergency fund. Your goal in the first year is not to get rich. It is to build a reliable customer base, establish a reputation for quality, and create systems that allow you to take on more work without dropping standards. By the end of this lesson, you should be able to write a one-page business plan for your plumbing enterprise, list your start-up costs, and identify your first ten potential customers. That is the foundation of a profitable plumbing business in Africa.

lessons.title: Module 10 Lesson 2: Water Supply Systems and Pipe Sizing for African Conditions
lessons.body: Water supply in Africa is rarely straightforward. In rural areas, people rely on boreholes, hand pumps, and rainwater harvesting. In peri-urban areas, communal taps and small-scale piped networks are common. In cities, municipal supply may be available only a few hours a day, forcing households to store water in tanks. As a plumber, you must understand how to design and install systems that work under these conditions. This lesson covers the fundamentals of water supply systems and pipe sizing, with practical examples you can apply on the job. Start with the source. A water supply system begins at the point where water enters the property. That could be a municipal connection, a borehole with a submersible pump, a rainwater tank, or a gravity-fed spring. Your first task is to measure the available pressure and flow rate. Pressure is measured in bars or meters of head. Flow rate is measured in liters per minute. You can use a simple pressure gauge and a bucket test. Attach the gauge to the nearest tap and open it fully. Note the pressure. Then fill a 10-liter bucket and time how long it takes. If it takes 30 seconds, the flow rate is 20 liters per minute. This information determines what fixtures and pipe sizes you can use. Next, understand pipe sizing. Pipes that are too small cause low pressure and noise. Pipes that are too large waste money and can allow water to stagnate. The goal is to select a pipe diameter that keeps water velocity between 0.5 and 1.5 meters per second. Higher velocities cause erosion and noise. Lower velocities allow sediment to settle. For a typical African household with one bathroom, one kitchen, and a small garden, a 20mm or 25mm main line is usually sufficient. For a guesthouse with ten rooms, you may need a 32mm or 40mm main line. Always calculate the peak demand. Peak demand is the total flow rate if all fixtures are used at once. In practice, not all fixtures are used simultaneously, so you apply a diversity factor. For a house with one bathroom, the peak demand might be 20 liters per minute. For a small hotel, it could be 100 liters per minute. Use these numbers to size the main line and the distribution pipes. Materials matter. In Africa, the most common pipe materials are PVC, PPR, and galvanized steel. PVC is cheap and easy to install but cannot handle hot water. PPR is more expensive but handles hot and cold water and is resistant to corrosion. Galvanized steel is strong but rusts over time and is difficult to repair. For hot water lines, use PPR or copper. For cold water lines, PVC or PPR are both acceptable. Always use the correct solvent cement for PVC and the correct fusion welding tools for PPR. Poor joints are the number one cause of leaks. Storage tanks are essential in most African settings. Even if you have a municipal connection, install a storage tank with a float valve. The tank fills when water is available and provides a buffer when supply stops. Size the tank based on daily consumption. A typical person uses 50 to 100 liters per day for drinking, cooking, and washing. A family of six needs at least 600 liters of storage. For a small guesthouse with twenty guests, you need at least 2000 liters. Install the tank on a raised platform or a stand to provide gravity pressure. A tank 5 meters above the outlet gives roughly 0.5 bar of pressure, which is enough for a shower but not for a washing machine. For higher pressure, use a booster pump. Pumps are another critical component. In borehole systems, you need a submersible pump that fits the borehole diameter and can lift water from the water level to the tank. Calculate the total head: the vertical distance from the water level to the tank, plus friction losses in the pipe, plus the pressure required at the outlet. A common mistake is to buy a pump that is too small, leading to low flow, or too large, leading to frequent cycling and high electricity bills. Use a pump with a pressure switch and a pressure tank to maintain steady pressure. Finally, test everything. After installation, pressurize the system and check for leaks. Run all fixtures simultaneously and measure the pressure at the furthest outlet. If pressure drops below 0.5 bar, you may need to increase pipe size or add a booster pump. Document your work with photos and a simple diagram. This helps you troubleshoot later and shows the customer that you are professional. By mastering water supply systems and pipe sizing, you can install systems that work reliably in African conditions, where supply is unpredictable and quality varies. That reliability is what customers pay for.

lessons.title: Module 10 Lesson 3: Drainage, Sewerage, and Sanitation Solutions
lessons.body: Sanitation is one of the biggest challenges in Africa. Many communities lack centralized sewerage, and where it exists, it is often overloaded. As a plumber, you will be called to install and repair septic tanks, soak pits, pit latrines, and small-bore sewer systems. This lesson gives you practical knowledge to design and maintain these systems safely and effectively. Start with the basics of drainage. Wastewater comes from three sources: blackwater from toilets, greywater from sinks, showers, and laundry, and stormwater from rain. In a well-designed system, these are kept separate. Blackwater goes to a septic tank or sewer. Greywater can go to a soak pit or a constructed wetland. Stormwater goes to a drainage channel or a soakaway. Mixing them causes overload and environmental pollution. The most common on-site system in Africa is the septic tank. A septic tank is a watertight chamber that separates solids from liquids. The solids settle at the bottom as sludge, while grease and scum float on top. The liquid in the middle flows out to a soak pit or drain field. For a household of six, a septic tank should be at least 2000 liters. For a school with 200 students, you need a tank of at least 10000 liters. The tank must have two compartments: the first for settling and the second for further digestion. The outlet should have a T-pipe or baffle to prevent scum from escaping. Never use a single-compartment tank for a large population. Soak pits and drain fields are where the liquid effluent is absorbed into the ground. A soak pit is a hole filled with stones or broken bricks, covered with soil. A drain field is a series of perforated pipes laid in trenches. The soil must be permeable. If the soil is clay, you need a raised bed or a mound system. Test the soil by digging a hole and filling it with water. If the water drains within 24 hours, the soil is suitable. If not, you need an alternative. In many African cities, pit latrines are still common. A pit latrine is a hole in the ground with a slab and a shelter. The pit should be at least 2 meters deep and 1 meter wide. The slab must be strong and have a drop hole with a cover to reduce flies and smell. When the pit fills, you can empty it using a vacuum truck or a manual pump. In dense settlements, emptying is difficult, so you should design pits with a removable cover and access for a hose. For new installations, consider a ventilated improved pit latrine, which uses a vent pipe to reduce odors and flies. Small-bore sewer systems are a good option for peri-urban areas. These systems use small-diameter pipes, typically 75mm to 100mm, laid at a shallow depth with a continuous gradient. They connect several households to a communal septic tank or a treatment plant. The advantage is lower cost and easier installation than conventional sewers. The disadvantage is that they require regular maintenance and cannot handle solid waste. Educate your customers not to flush plastics, sanitary pads, or rags. Blockages are the most common problem in drainage systems. Grease, hair, and food waste accumulate in pipes. To prevent blockages, install grease traps in kitchens and hair catchers in showers. Use the correct gradient: a 100mm pipe should fall 2cm per meter. A 50mm pipe should fall 3cm per meter. Too little slope causes solids to settle. Too much slope causes liquids to flow away too fast, leaving solids behind. When you unblock a drain, use a plunger, a drain snake, or a high-pressure jetter. Never use harsh chemicals because they damage pipes and harm the environment. Safety is critical. Sewage contains bacteria, viruses, and parasites. Always wear gloves, boots, and eye protection. Wash your hands with soap after every job. If you are working in a confined space, such as a septic tank, use a gas detector and never enter alone. Hydrogen sulfide and methane can kill. Ventilate the space before entering and have a rescue plan. Finally, think about sustainability. In Africa, water is scarce, so promote water-saving fixtures. A dual-flush toilet uses 3 to 6 liters per flush instead of 9 to 12 liters. A low-flow showerhead uses 6 to 8 liters per minute instead of 15. These small changes reduce the load on septic tanks and soak pits. Also, consider composting toilets for rural areas where water is unavailable. A composting toilet separates urine and feces and converts them into safe fertilizer. This is a growing market, especially for eco-lodges and off-grid homes. By mastering drainage, sewerage, and sanitation, you provide a service that directly improves public health. That is a powerful selling point. Customers will pay for a system that works and does not smell. Your reputation grows when you solve problems that others cannot.

lessons.title: Module 10 Lesson 4: Hot Water Systems and Geyser Installation
lessons.body: Hot water is a luxury in many African homes, but demand is growing. As incomes rise, more households install electric geysers, gas water heaters, and solar water heating systems. As a plumber, you can earn good money installing and servicing these systems. This lesson covers the types of hot water systems, how to install them safely, and how to troubleshoot common problems. Start with the three main types: electric storage geysers, gas instantaneous heaters, and solar water heaters. Electric geysers are the most common in urban Africa. They consist of a tank, a heating element, a thermostat, and a pressure relief valve. They store hot water for later use. A typical household geyser is 100 to 200 liters. Gas instantaneous heaters, also called tankless heaters, heat water only when a tap is opened. They are more energy-efficient but require a gas supply and proper ventilation. Solar water heaters use the sun to heat water in a collector and store it in an insulated tank. They have the lowest running cost but the highest upfront cost. When installing an electric geyser, safety is paramount. The geyser must be mounted on a strong wall or a platform that can support its weight when full. A 150-liter geyser weighs about 200 kilograms when full. Use stainless steel straps or brackets. The geyser must have a pressure relief valve and a vacuum breaker. The pressure relief valve opens if the pressure exceeds the rating, preventing an explosion. The vacuum breaker prevents the tank from collapsing when water is drained. Never block or remove these valves. The electrical connection must be done by a licensed electrician. The geyser must be on its own circuit with a circuit breaker and an earth leakage unit. The element and thermostat must match the voltage and wattage. In many African countries, voltage fluctuates, so install a surge protector. The water connections must use flexible hoses or copper pipes that can handle the temperature and pressure. Use dielectric unions to prevent galvanic corrosion between copper and steel. For gas heaters, ventilation is critical. Gas heaters produce carbon monoxide, which is deadly. Install the heater in a well-ventilated area, preferably outside the bathroom. Use a flue pipe to direct exhaust gases outside. The gas line must be installed by a licensed gas fitter. Use copper or stainless steel pipes, never plastic. Check for leaks with soapy water. Never use a flame to test for gas leaks. Solar water heaters require a different approach. The collector must face the equator: north in the southern hemisphere, south in the northern hemisphere. The tilt angle should equal the latitude of the location. For example, in Nairobi, latitude is about 1 degree south, so the tilt is nearly flat. In Johannesburg, latitude is 26 degrees south, so the tilt is 26 degrees. The tank must be above the collector for thermosiphon systems, or a pump must be used for forced circulation. The pipes must be insulated to prevent heat loss. In areas with hard water, install a water softener or use a scale inhibitor. Scale buildup reduces efficiency and can block pipes. Maintenance is where you make recurring income. Offer annual service contracts. For electric geysers, drain the tank to remove sediment, check the anode rod, and test the pressure relief valve. Replace the anode rod every two to three years. For gas heaters, clean the burner and check the gas pressure. For solar heaters, clean the collector and check the antifreeze if used. Charge a service fee and remind customers that regular maintenance extends the life of the system. Troubleshooting is a core skill. If a geyser has no hot water, check the circuit breaker, the thermostat, and the heating element. Use a multimeter to test continuity. If the water is too hot, the thermostat may be faulty. If the pressure relief valve is dripping, the pressure may be too high, or the valve may be worn. Replace it. If the water smells, the anode rod may be corroded. Replace it. If the geyser is leaking, it may be a loose connection or a cracked tank. A cracked tank cannot be repaired; it must be replaced. For gas heaters, if the water is not hot enough, check the gas pressure and the water flow rate. If the heater does not ignite, check the batteries, the igniter, and the gas supply. For solar heaters, if the water is not hot, check for airlocks, scale, or a faulty pump. Always follow the manufacturer instructions. Do not guess. Keep a copy of the manual for each model you install. Finally, price your work correctly. A geyser installation takes two to four hours. Charge for labor, materials, and a warranty. Offer a one-year warranty on your workmanship. That builds trust and reduces callbacks. In Africa, where reliable hot water is a sign of comfort and status, a well-installed system is a valuable asset. By mastering hot water systems, you add a high-value service to your plumbing business.

lessons.title: Module 10 Lesson 5: Maintenance, Customer Service, and Scaling Your Plumbing Enterprise
lessons.body: The difference between a plumber who struggles and a plumber who thrives is not technical skill alone. It is maintenance, customer service, and the ability to scale. This lesson focuses on the habits and systems that turn a one-person operation into a sustainable business that employs others and generates consistent profit. Start with preventive maintenance. Most plumbing emergencies are preventable. A burst pipe, a blocked drain, or a failed geyser usually gives warning signs: a slow leak, a discolored ceiling, a gurgling drain, or a rising water bill. Offer your customers a maintenance plan. For a small monthly fee, you visit their property once a quarter, inspect the plumbing, tighten connections, test valves, and clean drains. This gives you predictable income and reduces emergency call-outs. For commercial clients, such as hotels and schools, maintenance contracts are essential. They cannot afford to close because of a plumbing failure. Price the contract based on the size of the property and the number of fixtures. Include a response time guarantee, such as four hours for emergencies. That guarantee is worth more than the fee itself. Customer service is your competitive advantage. In Africa, many plumbers are known for being late, overcharging, or leaving a mess. Be different. Answer your phone. Confirm appointments. Arrive on time. Wear clean overalls. Use shoe covers or remove your shoes. Protect the floor with a drop cloth. Clean up after the job. Explain what you did and why. Give the customer a written report with photos. Follow up the next day to ask if everything is working. These small actions create loyal customers who refer you to others. Handle complaints professionally. If a customer is unhappy, listen without arguing. Apologize for the inconvenience. Fix the problem at no extra cost if it is your fault. If it is not your fault, explain clearly and offer a fair solution. Never argue on social media. Take the conversation offline. A satisfied customer tells three people. An angry customer tells thirty. Protect your reputation. Pricing is another area where many plumbers fail. Do not compete on price alone. Compete on value. If you are cheaper than everyone else, customers will suspect your quality. Instead, offer three tiers: a basic repair, a standard repair with a warranty, and a premium service with a maintenance plan. Most customers choose the middle option. That is where you make your profit. Always provide a written quote before starting work. Include labor, materials, and any additional costs. Get the customer to sign the quote. That prevents disputes. For larger jobs, ask for a deposit of 50 percent. That covers your material costs and ensures the customer is serious. Scaling your business requires systems. You cannot do everything yourself. Hire an apprentice. Train them in your methods. Pay them fairly and on time. Give them responsibility for small jobs while you handle larger ones. Use a simple job management system. A WhatsApp group with your team can work. Each morning, send the list of jobs. Each evening, ask for updates and photos. Track your income and expenses weekly. Know your numbers. If you do not know how much you earn per job, you cannot grow. Invest in tools. A good pipe wrench, a pressure tester, a drain snake, and a cordless drill save time and improve quality. Buy the best you can afford. Rent specialized tools, such as a high-pressure jetter or a thermal camera, until you can buy them. Keep your vehicle well maintained. A breakdown costs you money and damages your reputation. Marketing should be continuous. Ask every satisfied customer for a review. Post photos of your work on social media. Join local business associations. Offer a referral fee to real estate agents and hardware stores. Create a simple website or a Google Business profile. In Africa, word of mouth is powerful, but online reviews are becoming equally important. Finally, think about the future. The plumbing industry is changing. Water scarcity, climate change, and urbanization are creating new demands. Learn about rainwater harvesting, greywater recycling, and solar water heating. These are growth areas. Also, consider specializing. You can become the go-to plumber for hospitals, or for restaurants, or for apartment buildings. Specialists earn more than generalists. Set goals. In one year, you want a steady stream of repeat customers. In three years, you want a team of three to five plumbers and a vehicle. In five years, you want a registered company with a workshop and a reputation for excellence. Write these goals down. Review them every month. By combining technical skill with business discipline, you build a plumbing enterprise that not only survives but thrives in the African market. That is the ultimate goal of this module.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a plumbing vent stack?
options: A) To supply hot water to fixtures
B) To allow sewer gases to escape and equalize pressure
C) To drain wastewater from the building
quiz.explanation: Vent stacks allow sewer gases to escape safely and equalize air pressure in the drainage system so water flows properly.

quiz.q: Which material is most commonly used for modern residential water supply lines?
quiz.explanation: PEX is flexible, durable, and resistant to corrosion, making it a common choice for residential water supply lines.

quiz.q: What does a P-trap do in a plumbing fixture?
options: D) Holds a water seal to block sewer gases
quiz.explanation: A P-trap retains a small amount of water that creates a seal preventing sewer gases from entering the building.

quiz.q: What is the standard slope for a horizontal drain pipe of 3 inches or less?
quiz.explanation: A slope of 1/4 inch per foot is standard for drain pipes 3 inches or less to ensure proper flow.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to tighten a compression fitting on a supply line?
quiz.explanation: An adjustable wrench is used to tighten the nut on a compression fitting to create a watertight seal.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a backflow preventer?
options: B) To stop contaminated water from reversing into the clean supply
C) To reduce water hammer noise
quiz.explanation: A backflow preventer stops contaminated water from flowing backward into the potable water supply.

quiz.q: Which type of valve is best for throttling flow in a plumbing system?
quiz.explanation: Globe valves are designed for throttling and regulating flow, unlike gate or ball valves which are mainly for on or off control.

quiz.q: What should you do first before soldering copper pipe?
options: A) Apply flux to the outside of the pipe only
B) Turn on the water supply
C) Tighten all fittings by hand
D) Clean the pipe and fitting with emery cloth
quiz.explanation: Cleaning the pipe and fitting with emery cloth removes oxidation and ensures solder bonds properly.
